network.overall_strategy: The network integrates diverse prebiotic carbon and nitrogen sources (CO2, HCN, CH4, NH3), with conversion into simple organics (formaldehyde, ammonia, hydrogen cyanide, acetonitrile, glycolonitrile, methylamine, etc.) via hydrothermal and surface processes. Reductive amination, hydrolysis, Strecker-type reactions, and radical chemistry contribute multiple plausible routes. Some pathways merge intermediates derived from HCN and formaldehyde, while others use Strecker synthesis with aldehydes and ammonia or hydrothermal catalysis. This results in 10 distinct, literature-supported and chemically plausible synthesis pathways, traversing hydrothermal, surface, and biochemical/prebiotic environments, converging on glycine formation.

reactions.name: CO2 reduction to formaldehyde
reactions.mechanism: Reduction of CO2 to formaldehyde on FeS surfaces using H2 as electron donor.
reactions.reasoning: Supported by hydrothermal vent simulation experiments showing FeS-catalyzed reduction of CO2 to organics (Cody et al., 2000; Huber & Wächtershäuser, 1997).

reactions.name: HCN formation from CH4, NH3 and UV irradiation
reactions.mechanism: Photolysis of methane and ammonia in presence of UV to yield HCN.
reactions.reasoning: Supported by Miller–Urey-type classic prebiotic chemistry (Miller, 1953; Sutherland, 2016).

reactions.name: Formaldehyde cyanohydrin formation (Glycolonitrile synthesis)

conditions.other: Evaporitic pool, borate present stabilizes HCHO

reactions.mechanism: Nucleophilic addition of HCN to formaldehyde forms glycolonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Cyanohydrin formation is well documented under prebiotic conditions (Abelson, 1966; Ritson & Sutherland, 2012).

reactions.name: Strecker synthesis with glycolonitrile yields aminoacetonitrile
reactions.mechanism: Glycolonitrile reacts with ammonia to yield aminoacetonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Demonstrated in prebiotic simulations and wet-dry cycles; enhanced by mineral catalysis (Friche et al., 1975; Saladino et al., 2012).

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of aminoacetonitrile to glycine
reactions.mechanism: Hydrolytic conversion of nitrile to carboxyl group.
reactions.reasoning: Hydrolysis of aminoacetonitrile to glycine under mild acidic, mineral-rich conditions (Sánchez et al., 1967; Saladino et al., 2012).

reactions.name: Formamide hydrolysis from HCN
reactions.mechanism: Hydration and hydrolysis of HCN and formaldehyde to formamide.
reactions.reasoning: Modelled in prebiotic reaction scenarios, mineral surfaces expedite hydrolysis (Saladino et al., 2007).

reactions.name: Reductive amination of glyoxylate by ammonia
reactions.mechanism: Ammonia reacts with an aldehyde (representing glyoxylate here, simplified as formaldehyde) and is reduced to glycine equivalent.
reactions.reasoning: Although direct literature for formaldehyde to glycine is rare, FeS-catalyzed amination and reductive amination are prebiotically viable (Huber & Wächtershäuser, 1998).

reactions.name: Aminoacetonitrile formation from acetonitrile
reactions.mechanism: Amination of acetonitrile to form aminoacetonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: FeS surfaces catalyze amination and hydration reactions (He et al., 2010, speculative for this exact transformation but consistent with FeS catalysis).

reactions.name: Hydrothermal acetonitrile synthesis from methane and HCN
reactions.mechanism: Reductive coupling/amination of methane with HCN.
reactions.reasoning: Trace acetonitrile found in hydrothermal simulation mixtures; plausible with Ni/Fe catalysis (Rushdi & Simoneit, 2001).

reactions.name: Amine transfer and rearrangement: formamide + formaldehyde
reactions.mechanism: Condensation forms aminoethanol (proposed as an intermediate).
reactions.reasoning: Aminoethanol formation from formaldehyde and amide under dehydration on mineral surfaces is plausible (Oró, 1961; speculative based on amine chemistry).

reactions.name: Aminoethanol oxidation to aminoacetaldehyde
reactions.mechanism: Partial UV oxidation of aminoethanol to aminoacetaldehyde.
reactions.reasoning: UV-promoted oxidations and dehydrogenations plausible on the prebiotic Earth (Patel et al., 2015, as a plausible but speculative transformation).

reactions.name: Aminoacetaldehyde conversion to glycine
reactions.mechanism: Amine transfer/hydrolysis forms glycine from aminoacetaldehyde and ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Aminoacetaldehyde conversion to amino acids by hydrolysis/ammonolysis, shown in surface prebiotic experiments (Saladino et al., 2012).

reactions.name: Methanimine synthesis from methane and ammonia (radical/thermal)
reactions.mechanism: Thermal/radical chemistry drives methanimine formation from methane and ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Methanimine detected in simulation experiments (McCollom, 2013; hydrothermal synthesis plausible).

reactions.name: Methanimine conversion to aminoacetonitrile (via addition to HCN)
reactions.reasoning: Aminonitrile synthesis from imines and HCN is plausible; established in wet-dry cycles and photochemistry (Saladino et al., 2012; speculative for this direct transformation).

pathways.name: Strecker pathway via HCN and formaldehyde
pathways.description: Formaldehyde and HCN combine to form glycolonitrile, which reacts with ammonia to give aminoacetonitrile, then hydrolyzed to glycine.

pathways.name: Hydrothermal acetonitrile–aminoacetonitrile–glycine pathway
pathways.description: Methane and HCN form acetonitrile in hydrothermal conditions; amination yields aminoacetonitrile, hydrolysis leads to glycine.

pathways.name: Direct reductive amination pathway
pathways.description: Hydrothermal FeS catalysis enables conversion of formaldehyde and ammonia to glycine.

pathways.name: Formamide–aminoethanol–aminoacetaldehyde route
pathways.description: Formamide and formaldehyde form aminoethanol, oxidized to aminoacetaldehyde, which is converted to glycine.

pathways.name: Methanimine–aminoacetonitrile Strecker variant
pathways.description: Methanimine is formed from methane and ammonia, reacts with HCN to form aminoacetonitrile, then hydrolyzed to glycine.

pathways.name: Photochemical HCN from CH4/NH3 – glycolonitrile Strecker
pathways.description: Surface UV production of HCN from methane/ammonia feeds classic glycolonitrile Strecker sequence.

pathways.name: Surface-catalyzed formamide pathway
pathways.description: HCN and formaldehyde yield formamide, which can participate in C–N bond-forming aminoethanol chemistry.

pathways.name: HCN–methanimine Strecker–glycine
pathways.description: Methanimine generated from methane/ammonia reacts with HCN to aminoacetonitrile, hydrolyzed to glycine.

pathways.name: Wet-dry cycling aminoacetaldehyde pathway
pathways.description: Aminoethanol from surface chemistry is oxidized to aminoacetaldehyde, which reacts with ammonia to yield glycine.

pathways.name: Hydrolysis of aminoacetonitrile from HCN-methanimine route
pathways.description: Alternate route through methanimine plus HCN direct to aminoacetonitrile and hydrolytic cleavage to glycine.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: P1 follows the classical Strecker pathway, but mass conservation is problematic: rxn_004 (missing H2O as product) and rxn_005 (unbalanced with no clear fix) violate atom balance. Reaction mechanisms are chemically plausible, and environmental parameters fit. Target is reached, but overall pathway undermined by poor conservation in steps 2 and 3.
suggestions: Fix atom and charge conservation in rxn_004 (add H2O product)
Correct stoichiometry for hydrolysis in rxn_005 or clarify mechanism

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Chemical feasibility diminished by unbalanced reactions: rxn_009 (suggests loss of 2H), rxn_008 (missing H2 product or HCN reactant), and rxn_005 (no way to fully balance). Plausibility for acetonitrile and aminoacetonitrile synthesis from prebiotic feedstocks exists but steps must conserve mass for pathway validity.
suggestions: Balance reactions by adding H2 or NH3 where required
Provide explicit reaction mechanisms or literature precedent for these conversions

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Reductive amination involving HCHO and NH3 to glycine (rxn_007) is unbalanced and questionable (missing C/O, H2 or CO), lowering chemical feasibility. Hydrolysis (rxn_005) has no adequate balancing. Pathway is plausible at a high level but does not pass detailed chemical scrutiny.
suggestions: Specify missing balancing species (e.g., H2, CO) in rxn_007
Review mechanism for direct conversion of intermediates to glycine

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Pathway explores interesting amine-transfer and rearrangement mechanisms, but rxn_006 is unbalanced (C deficit), rxn_010 (needs CO2 as product), rxn_011 (H2 missing), and rxn_012 (not balanceable) all undermine chemistry. Environmental staging is largely reasonable but intermediary chemistry needs revision.
suggestions: Explicitly balance reactions by adding/removing small molecules (H2, CO2)
Check literature support for these conversion mechanisms
Clarify the oxidative/biochemical transition in rxn_011

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Methanimine and Strecker reactions are plausible at high level, but atom balance for rxn_014 (unchecked/parsing issues, likely missing balancing species) and rxn_005 (unresolvable) reduces validity; reaction conditions seem consistent, but chemical detail must improve.
suggestions: Provide balanceable reaction schemes for methanimine addition
Specify mechanism and byproducts in aminoacetonitrile hydrolysis

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Photochemical HCN formation (rxn_002) is plausible with added H2, but Strecker-type steps suffer from the same unbalance as P1. Pathway execution is appropriately environmental but chemistry must be rigorously checked for mass/charge conservation.
suggestions: Add H2 as product in rxn_002
Balance all Strecker-related reactions with water or other expected byproducts

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Complex route via amine transfer and hydrolysis but suffers cumulative mass conservation issues in rxn_006, rxn_010, rxn_011, rxn_012, with rxn_007 also needing additional balancing. Inconsistent chemistry outweighs environmental/historical plausibility.
suggestions: Rewrite amine transfer and oxidation steps with correct balancing
Justify reaction conditions and intermediates with literature

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Combination Strecker/Reductive pathways are creative but fail mass conservation (rxn_004, rxn_005, rxn_014) as above. Mechanistic ambiguity in aminoacetonitrile hydrolysis continues to be a key shortcoming.
suggestions: Clarify and balance each step, referencing established Strecker hydrolysis literature
Fix intermediate chemistries for atom economy

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Wet-dry cycling route interesting, but oxidation (rxn_011) and conversion to glycine (rxn_012) are not balanced according to the balance check. Each step needs clearly identified byproducts for full chemical coherence.
suggestions: Balance redox steps explicitly
Reference plausible catalytic or environmental processes that support these conversions

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Hydrolysis of aminoacetonitrile (rxn_005) not chemically balanced, and methanimine steps (rxn_013, rxn_014) lack explicit balancing, although plausible as reaction classes. Pathway success thus limited by unresolved chemistry.
suggestions: Clarify fate of H, N, and O atoms in all methanimine and hydrolysis steps
Provide complete equations for unparsed reactions

evaluation.network_feedback: The network offers diverse, literature-informed and environment-consistent glycine prebiotic syntheses, but suffers from pervasive and serious mass/charge conservation failures in nearly every pathway (as identified in the deterministic atom/charge check). Most reactions are plausible in broad mechanistic outlines but require explicit balancing: missing water, H2, or other small species compromise chemical feasibility and overall network validity. To achieve approval, reaction equations must be rigorously revised to ensure atom and charge conservation, and all unparsed molecules/intermediates (especially methanimine/aminonitrile steps) clarified with explicit structures and side products noted. Only after such correction can this synthesis network be considered chemically viable.
